title: Bowsher v. Synar (1986)
summary: Congress cannot give executive functions to an officer whom Congress alone can remove, because that would let Congress control the execution of the laws.
notes:
Key line: To permit the execution of the laws to be vested in an officer answerable only to Congress would, in practical terms, reserve in Congress control over the execution of the laws. (Chief Justice Burger)

Citation: 478 U.S. 714 (1986).

sections.Parties: The appellant in No. 85-1377 was Charles A. Bowsher, Comptroller General of the United States, head of the General Accounting Office. The United States Senate and Speaker Thomas O'Neill of the House of Representatives were appellants in the companion cases. The appellees were Representative Mike Synar of Oklahoma and eleven other members of Congress, the National Treasury Employees Union, and one of the Union's members whose cost-of-living benefit increase was suspended by the statute. Lloyd Cutler argued for the Comptroller General. The dispute concerned the Comptroller General's role in the automatic deficit reduction process of the Balanced Budget and Emergency Deficit Control Act of 1985.
sections.Material Facts: The Balanced Budget and Emergency Deficit Control Act of 1985, known as the Gramm-Rudman-Hollings Act, set maximum deficit amounts for fiscal years 1986 through 1991, falling to zero in 1991. If the projected deficit exceeded the target by more than a set sum, section 251 required across-the-board cuts. The OMB and CBO Directors were to estimate the deficit and compute reductions and report to the Comptroller General, who would resolve differences and report his conclusions to the President. The President was required to issue a sequestration order carrying out the Comptroller General's reductions, effective unless Congress legislated cuts within a fixed time. Under statutes dating from 1921, the Comptroller General, though nominated by the President and confirmed by the Senate, may be removed only by impeachment or by joint resolution of Congress for permanent disability, inefficiency, neglect of duty, malfeasance, or a felony or conduct involving moral turpitude.
sections.Procedural History: Within hours of President Reagan signing the Act on December 12, 1985, Congressman Synar, who had voted against it, filed suit in the United States District Court for the District of Columbia seeking a declaration that the Act was unconstitutional. The National Treasury Employees Union filed a similar action, and the cases were consolidated before a three-judge court under the Act's expedited review provision. The District Court held that the Comptroller General's role in the deficit reduction process violated the separation of powers because he was removable only by Congress and was exercising executive functions, 626 F. Supp. 1374 (1986). Direct appeals followed. The Supreme Court heard argument on April 23, 1986, and decided the case on July 7, 1986, affirming by a vote of seven to two. Chief Justice Burger wrote for the Court.
sections.Issue: Did the appellees have standing, given that the Act suspended scheduled cost-of-living increases for a Union member? On the merits, may Congress assign to the Comptroller General, an officer removable only at the initiative of Congress by joint resolution or impeachment, the function under section 251 of determining the spending reductions that the President must carry out? That question required the Court to decide whether the Comptroller General is subservient to Congress by reason of the removal provisions and whether the functions section 251 gives him are executive in nature. If section 251 was invalid, the Court also had to choose a remedy between striking the removal provision and enforcing the Act's fallback.
sections.Holding: The Union member's loss of a benefit increase gave standing, so the Court did not consider the standing of the Union itself or the members of Congress. Section 251 violates the Constitution's command that Congress play no direct role in executing the laws. Congress may not reserve for itself the power to remove an officer charged with executing the laws except by impeachment; the joint resolution procedure, with its broad grounds, makes the Comptroller General answerable to Congress. His duties under section 251, interpreting the Act, exercising judgment about estimates and binding the President, are executive. Congress therefore retained control over execution of the Act, which the Constitution forbids. The remedy is the fallback procedure of section 274(f), which Congress itself prescribed. Judgment affirmed.
sections.Reasoning: Chief Justice Burger began with the structural premise of Myers v. United States and Humphrey's Executor: the President's power to remove executive officers is a part of executive power, and Congress may limit that power in certain cases, but Congress cannot itself hold the removal power over executive officers. INS v. Chadha had held that Congress can affect the execution of the laws only by passing new legislation through both Houses and presentment. Combining those principles, the Court concluded that to permit an officer answerable only to Congress to execute the laws would in practical terms reserve to Congress control over execution. The Comptroller General is such an officer. The 1921 statute lets Congress remove him for inefficiency, neglect of duty or malfeasance, terms broad enough to cover any act Congress dislikes, and the legislative history shows Congress intended him to be its agent. The Court then examined what section 251 asks the Comptroller General to do. He must interpret the Act to decide what budget data and assumptions to use, and his report binds the President, who must issue a sequestration order matching it. Interpreting a law enacted by Congress to implement the legislative mandate is the very essence of executing the law. As for remedy, Congress had anticipated the problem and provided the fallback in section 274(f), and the Court gave effect to that intent rather than invalidating the 1921 removal provision.

topics.lrs-s-congressional-control: Congress retained a direct removal mechanism over an officer assigned binding executive duties.
topics.lrs-s-severability: Blackmun’s proposed remedy would sever the removal provision rather than disable the new function.

learning.separateOpinions: Seven to two. Justice Stevens, joined by Justice Marshall, concurred in the judgment: the Comptroller General is an agent of Congress, and Congress may not delegate policymaking to its own agent outside the bicameral and presentment process, whether or not the functions are labeled executive. Justice White dissented, calling the removal provision a dormant, carefully circumscribed power that requires either the President's signature or a two-thirds override and arguing that the Court's formalism destroyed a workable statute. Justice Blackmun dissented separately; he would have struck the 1921 removal provision rather than the 1985 Act.
